clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, typically pure (uncomplicated) hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by heterozygous SLC33A1 mutations encoding the endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1.
Originally delineated in a large Han Chinese kindred; manifests as a length-dependent corticospinal tract degeneration.
Age of onset is strikingly variable, ranging from early childhood to mid-adulthood even within a single family.
Core signs are slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses and a spastic gait, with the upper limbs characteristically spared.
Incomplete penetrance and intrafamilial variability are recognised, so obligate carriers may appear unaffected.
Urinary urgency can emerge later, but sensation and cognition remain preserved in the pure phenotype.
Biallelic loss-of-function SLC33A1 change causes a distinct severe congenital neurodegenerative syndrome with cataracts and hearing loss, which must not be conflated with dominant SPG42.
Diagnosis rests on genetic testing; no routine acetyl-CoA transporter assay exists in clinical practice.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG42 arises from mutation in SLC33A1, which encodes acetyl-coenzyme A transporter 1 (AT-1), an endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein that imports cytosolic acetyl-CoA into the ER lumen to supply the acetyl donor for N-epsilon-lysine acetylation of nascent membrane and secretory proteins. The recognised dominant allele (a serine-to-arginine substitution) is thought to act by a dominant-negative or gain-of-function mechanism that perturbs ER protein acetylation, proteostasis and autophagy; the very long corticospinal axons are selectively vulnerable to this metabolic and trafficking stress, producing a distal, length-dependent axonopathy that clinically presents as progressive lower-limb spasticity.
additionalDifferentials: SPG4 (SPAST/spastin) - the commonest autosomal dominant pure HSP
Other dominant pure subtypes: SPG6 (NIPA1), SPG8 (WASHC5), SPG10 (KIF5A), SPG12 (RTN2)
Primary lateral sclerosis and early amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Dopa-responsive dystonia and spastic diplegic cerebral palsy in childhood-onset cases
Acquired myelopathies from vitamin B12 or copper deficiency, or HTLV-1 infection
additionalInvestigations: Targeted SLC33A1 sequencing within a hereditary spastic paraplegia gene panel or exome sequencing
MRI of the brain and whole spine to exclude structural, demyelinating or compressive myelopathy
Nerve conduction studies and EMG, expected to be normal in the pure form and useful to exclude a neuropathy
Serum vitamin B12, copper, caeruloplasmin, very-long-chain fatty acids and HTLV-1 serology to exclude treatable or infective mimics
Motor and somatosensory evoked potentials to document central conduction delay
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis when an acquired inflammatory myelopathy is plausible
Family segregation analysis and genetic counselling
redFlags: A distinct sensory level, rapidly evolving bladder or bowel dysfunction, or back pain suggesting a compressive or structural cord lesion rather than HSP
Rapidly progressive or markedly asymmetric weakness raising concern for motor neurone disease
Cognitive decline, cataracts or deafness pointing to the recessive SLC33A1 syndrome or an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Pure SPG42 is generally slowly progressive, with ambulation preserved for years to decades and a normal life expectancy, although walking aids may eventually become necessary.
pitfalls: Assuming any SLC33A1 variant is causal, as the pathogenicity of dominant HSP alleles has been debated and requires careful interpretation with family segregation
Confusing dominant SPG42 with the severe recessive biallelic SLC33A1 neurodegeneration syndrome
Labelling static-appearing childhood-onset cases as cerebral palsy
Omitting exclusion of treatable mimics such as vitamin B12 or copper deficiency before committing to a genetic label
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, with botulinum toxin for focal lower-limb spasticity
Regular physiotherapy, stretching and provision of orthoses and walking aids to maintain the spastic gait
Bladder management with antimuscarinic therapy for urinary urgency emerging later in the course
Surveillance for gait deterioration, falls and contractures with orthotic and orthopaedic review
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and strikingly variable onset, offering testing to relatives
Multidisciplinary neurology, physiotherapy and rehabilitation input
